paragraphs.text: This cake was made from [Yiwu](greater-yiwu:where-it-is) leaf, grown in the north of Mengla County in Xishuangbanna, on the east side of the Lancang River. The area is one of the old Six Famous Tea Mountains, and its town has long been where the surrounding villages bring their tea to be gathered and processed.

The leaf was made into [ripe pu’er](shou:definition) by [wet piling](shou:wet-piling). It was wetted and heaped so that microbes could warm it from within, covered to hold that heat and turned about once a week to let air in, then dried after one to two months and pressed into a cake in 2015. The pile exists to give, in weeks, the change that raw pu’er only reaches after years of keeping.

At eleven years it has passed into what the trade counts as [aged ripe pu’er](shou:age-aged). The leaf still changes slowly with the air and moisture around it, which is why storage matters as much as the years.

brewing.text: From a cake, brick or tuo, ease a piece off along the edge with a pick rather than snapping it. Whole leaves give up their flavour steadily; broken ones release it all at once and cloud the cup. Ripe pu’er takes boiling water: fermented, tightly packed leaf needs full heat to open, and it does not scald the way green tea can. A common start is about 7 grams to 100 ml and one quick rinse, which wakes the leaf and carries off dust and any pile smell. Then short steeps that lengthen as the leaf opens, so the cup stays clear rather than heavy; it gives eight or more good cups.

notice.text: A smooth, deep cup with woody, date-like or medicinal notes, which the trade calls aged aroma.
